check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, clear introduction, confirms identity and relationship.
Speaks to and engages Liam directly as well as the parent:

kids.x: Uses simple language, gestures or his communication cues.
Does not talk about him as though he is not present.

check.x: Empathic, non-judgemental approach that acknowledges the parent's exhaustion.
History
Characterises the behavioural change:

kids.x: Onset, timing (afternoons), pattern and progression.
Aggression to others and self-injury, including hitting his tummy.
Sleep disturbance and reduced appetite.

check.x: Explicitly looks for a physical cause before attributing the change to the intellectual disability or behaviour:

kids.x: Pain: asks about face or mouth pulling, chewing, abdominal hitting and the last dental review.
Bowel habit: frequency, stool consistency, straining, soiling or overflow.
Reflux symptoms.
Urinary symptoms (UTI).
Fever, injury, other illness, seizures.

check.x: Takes a medication history and reviews for adverse effects and polypharmacy:

kids.x: Identifies the risperidone dose increase 6 weeks ago.
Asks about extrapyramidal effects (stiffness, drooling, restlessness, tremor).
Asks about other medicines (melatonin) and anything recently started or stopped.

check.x: Explores recent changes in his situation:

kids.x: Loss of his favourite teacher's aide and the change of bus driver.
Changes in routine or carers at home.

check.x: Sensitively screens for abuse, neglect and carer stress:

kids.x: Asks who else cares for Liam, about unexplained injuries and fearfulness.
Asks about the parent's own coping and supports.

check.x: Brief background history: cause of the disability, development, epilepsy, allergies, immunisations.
Explores the parent's concerns and expectations (worried he will be kept home from school).
Examination
Explains the examination to Liam, uses distraction (his tablet) and keeps the parent with him.
Vital signs, weight and height.
Abdomen for faecal loading (firm mass in the left iliac fossa, mildly tender) and perianal inspection for soiling or a fissure, without a routine rectal examination.
Mouth and teeth with a torch (carious, tender lower left molar with gum swelling) and the neck nodes.
Skin survey for bruising or injury (knuckle callus and abdominal redness from self-hitting, no bruises).
Neurological examination for extrapyramidal effects: tone (cogwheel rigidity), tremor, drooling, restlessness (akathisia), gait.
Ears, throat, chest and a musculoskeletal screen, and asks for a urine dipstick and BGL.
Interpretation
Observations and growth normal, no fever; concentrated urine (specific gravity 1.025) fits his low fluid intake, with no sign of UTI; BGL normal.
Identifies constipation with faecal loading and dental pain (probable dental abscess) as the most likely drivers of the behaviour change.
Recognises the contribution of risperidone (the dose increase, extrapyramidal effects including akathisia that can look like agitation, and constipation) and the stress of losing the familiar aide.
Considers other causes: reflux, UTI, endocrine (for example thyroid), epilepsy, sleep problems, abuse.
Interprets the SDQ correctly:

kids.x: The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire is a brief behavioural screening tool for children and adolescents, with parent and teacher versions.
It covers emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity and inattention, peer problems and prosocial behaviour.
The total of 24 is in the abnormal range, highest for conduct and hyperactivity: it shows how marked his difficulties are now (the teacher and the history say this is new), not why.
It is a screening tool only, not diagnostic, and does not exclude a physical cause; it is interpreted after medical causes are addressed and can be repeated to monitor change.

check.x: Management
Treats the physical causes first rather than starting a behaviour plan or increasing the antipsychotic:

kids.x: Constipation: disimpaction with an oral macrogol, increasing the number of sachets each day by his age band as in the RCH constipation guideline's disimpaction table until the stools are soft and runny, then maintenance for months, with more fluids and fibre and a toileting routine.

Urgent dental referral (paediatric or special needs dentistry, possibly treatment under anaesthetic) and regular analgesia: paracetamol 15 mg/kg = 465 mg for 31 kg up to 4 times a day, and ibuprofen 10 mg/kg = 310 mg for 31 kg 8-hourly with food.
Considers treating reflux if symptomatic.

check.x: Reviews the medication:

kids.x: Contacts the prescriber to reduce the risperidone towards the previous dose rather than stopping it abruptly.
Plans a review of the ongoing indication for an antipsychotic and does not add another sedating medicine.

check.x: Liaises with the school about transition support, familiar staff and visual supports, and asks that the behaviour plan wait until the physical causes are treated.
Offers carer support and respite options, with GP-led follow-up.
Explains to the parent in plain language that pain or discomfort may be causing the behaviour, responds to "Do you really think he might be in pain?" with empathy, and checks understanding.
Safety netting

Tells the parent to return or go to the Emergency Department for facial or neck swelling, fever, vomiting, a swollen or very painful tummy, no bowel motion despite the laxatives, or new severe stiffness or abnormal movements; call 000 if anyone is at immediate risk of harm.
Arranges early review in 1 to 2 weeks to check bowels, pain, behaviour and medication, sooner if worse, and plans to repeat the SDQ once the physical causes are treated.

desc: This station involves a focused history from the parent of a 10-year-old boy with intellectual disability and a recent change in behaviour, and a focused examination, then interpreting his observations, bedside tests and a teacher-completed Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, and outlining management and safety netting.
explain:
Behavioural change in a child with intellectual disability

Children with intellectual disability often cannot describe pain or discomfort, so distress is expressed through behaviour. A sudden change (aggression, self-injury, withdrawal, sleep or appetite change) should prompt a search for a physical cause first, rather than being attributed to the disability or to "challenging behaviour" (diagnostic overshadowing).

What to look for

  • Physical causes: pain (including dental), constipation, reflux, UTI, endocrine problems such as thyroid disease, epilepsy, sensory problems, sleep disorders. Ask carers about bowel habit specifically, as constipation is common and often missed.

  • Medications: review for side effects and polypharmacy. Antipsychotics such as risperidone can cause extrapyramidal effects (stiffness, tremor, drooling, akathisia), constipation, sedation and weight gain. Akathisia can itself look like agitation and lead to further dose escalation.

  • Psychosocial factors: abuse, neglect, carer stress, and recent changes such as the loss of a trusted support person, new routines or transport changes.

  • Talk to the patient directly using simple language, gestures and visual supports, and always include their carers' observations.

In this case

Liam has faecal loading (made worse by risperidone, low fluids and low fibre) and a carious, tender lower left molar with gum swelling, both painful; his self-hitting of the abdomen and pulling at the left side of his face point to them. His risperidone was increased and he has mild cogwheel rigidity, tremor, drooling and akathisia. He has also lost a trusted aide. All of these plausibly contribute to his behaviour, and a behaviour plan or more antipsychotic would address none of them.

Interpreting the Part 2 results

His observations are normal and he has no fever. The urine is concentrated, which fits his low fluid intake, and shows no sign of infection. The teacher SDQ total of 24 is in the abnormal range, driven by conduct and hyperactivity scores, but it only shows how marked his difficulties are now, which the teacher's comment and the history say is new; it cannot say why, and the high hyperactivity score may partly be akathisia. The SDQ was not designed for children with intellectual disability (the Developmental Behaviour Checklist was), so it is best used after the medical assessment and repeated to monitor change once the physical causes are treated.

Management

Disimpaction with an oral macrogol, increasing the daily number of sachets by age band as in the RCH constipation guideline's table until the stools are soft and runny, followed by maintenance for months with fluids, fibre and a toileting routine. Urgent dental care (often special needs dentistry, sometimes under anaesthetic) with regular weight-based analgesia: paracetamol 15 mg/kg (465 mg for 31 kg) and ibuprofen 10 mg/kg (310 mg for 31 kg). A medication review with the prescriber, reducing the risperidone gradually rather than stopping it. Support for the school transition, carer support and early review.

Safety netting

Facial or neck swelling or fever suggests a spreading dental infection; vomiting, a swollen or very painful abdomen or no bowel motion despite laxatives needs review; new severe stiffness or abnormal movements after a medication change needs urgent assessment. Review in 1 to 2 weeks.

The SDQ

The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire is a brief behavioural screening questionnaire for children and adolescents with parent and teacher versions. It covers emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity and inattention, peer problems and prosocial behaviour. It is a screening and monitoring tool, not a diagnostic test, and is only interpretable once physical and situational causes have been considered.
focus: Child with intellectual disability and behavioural change
guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. In Part 2 the examiner hands over the observations, bedside tests and teacher SDQ, and asks the questions in order.

A high-performing candidate talks to Liam as well as the parent and treats a sudden change in behaviour in a child who cannot communicate as pain or illness until proven otherwise. They ask about bowels, teeth, reflux and urinary symptoms, review the risperidone dose increase and its extrapyramidal and constipating effects, and sensitively screen for abuse, neglect, carer stress and the loss of the teacher's aide. They examine the abdomen, mouth, skin and for extrapyramidal signs, find the faecal loading and the carious molar, and treat constipation and dental pain with weight-based analgesia and a medication review before any behavioural intervention. They explain the SDQ as a screening and monitoring tool that shows how marked the difficulties are but not their cause.

A borderline candidate takes a history focused on the behaviour alone, accepts the school's framing and moves towards a behaviour plan, SDQ or psychiatry referral without searching for pain, constipation or medication effects. They may not talk to Liam, may overlook the risperidone dose change or the extrapyramidal signs, and may describe the SDQ incorrectly or treat it as a diagnosis.
patient:
Role: You are the parent of Liam Nguyen, aged 10. You are tired and worried. Liam is in the room, sitting with his tablet; he cannot answer questions. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. Not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

Opening line: "He has become so angry and aggressive. The school says he needs a behaviour plan, but this isn't like him."

The behaviour (give when asked):

  • Started about 3 weeks ago and has slowly got worse.
  • Hitting staff and other children at school, throwing objects, screaming, mostly in the afternoons.
  • Only if asked about self-injury or what he does when upset: he hits his own tummy with his fist and presses his belly against the edge of furniture.
  • Only if asked about eating or his face or mouth: he pulls at the left side of his face, refuses crunchy foods and chews less.
  • Sleep disrupted, waking crying at night 3 to 4 times a week. Eating less over the past fortnight.
  • No fever, vomiting or cough. No injury or fall that you know of. No seizures.

Bowels and bladder (only if specifically asked):

  • Bowels open every 4 to 5 days, hard pellet stools; he strains and cries. He used to go every day. Soiled underwear twice in the past week, which you thought was "him being naughty".
  • A little more wetting than usual; no change in urine smell or colour. You are not sure if it hurts him to pass urine.
  • Drinks little water; fussy diet, low in fibre.
  • Sometimes arches his back and brings up food after meals (reflux since infancy, no current treatment).

Medicines (give when asked):

  • Risperidone, started by a previous specialist 8 months ago for aggression; the dose was increased 6 weeks ago and is now 0.5 mg twice a day.
  • Only if asked about side effects or changes: since the increase he seems stiffer, drools more and is restless, unable to sit still.
  • Melatonin 2 mg at night. No other medicines. You did not know risperidone can cause constipation.

Background:

  • Moderate intellectual disability, cause unknown (genetic testing normal). Born at term. No epilepsy. Immunisations up to date. No allergies.
  • Last dental check more than 2 years ago because he does not tolerate it.

Home and school (give when asked about changes):

  • Lives with both parents and a younger sister. You are "at your limit" with the lack of sleep, but deny any harm to Liam and have no concerns about anyone else who cares for him.
  • 4 weeks ago his favourite teacher's aide, who had worked with him for 3 years, left the school. A relief aide has taken over. His school bus driver changed at the same time.
  • No change in routine at home, no new carers, no unexplained bruises. Liam is not fearful of any particular person.

Concerns and expectations: you want the behaviour to stop and are worried the school will ask you to keep him home. If the candidate suggests a physical cause: "Do you really think he might be in pain? He can't tell us."

Cues: if the candidate greets or engages Liam directly (simple words, gestures, letting him keep his tablet), he calms, looks at them and lets them examine him. If the candidate blames you or labels Liam as "just behavioural", you become upset. Interrupt if medical jargon is used.
points: In a child with intellectual disability who cannot report symptoms, a sudden behavioural change is pain or illness until proven otherwise: look for dental pain, constipation, reflux, UTI and endocrine causes.

Always review medications for side effects (for example extrapyramidal effects and constipation with antipsychotics) and polypharmacy, and consider abuse, neglect, carer stress and recent changes such as losing a support worker.
Ask carers specifically about bowel habit and speak to the patient directly.

The SDQ is a brief parent/teacher behavioural screening questionnaire covering emotional, conduct, hyperactivity/inattention, peer and prosocial domains; it is not diagnostic and does not replace a medical assessment.
Treat the physical causes first (disimpaction, dental care with weight-based analgesia, a medication review) before any behaviour plan, and review early.

stem: You are a GP. Liam Nguyen, a 10-year-old boy with moderate intellectual disability, is brought in by his parent because his behaviour has become much worse over the past 3 weeks. He is largely non-verbal and uses a few single words and gestures. The school has suggested he needs a behaviour management plan.
tasks: Take a focused history from the parent, engaging Liam as well, and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Liam's observations, bedside test results and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) completed by his teacher. Interpret them, including the role of the SDQ, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Sudden aggression in a boy with intellectual disability

part2.lead: Here are Liam's observations and bedside tests, and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire his teacher completed last week.

handover.label: Observations and growth
handover.result: Weight 31 kg and height 138 cm, both around the 50th centile.

rows.note: Sitting with his tablet, restless in the chair.
Pulse oximeter reading during the abdominal examination: grimacing and pulling away when the left lower abdomen is pressed.

handover.model:
Written out, not charted: a GP visit has no observation chart. HR 92, BP 102/64, RR 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C and a brisk capillary refill are all normal for a 10-year-old, and weight and height are both on the 50th centile. The heart rate rose to 104 with grimacing during the abdominal examination: still normal, but in keeping with pain.

No fever or systemic upset, so no sign of a spreading dental infection or another acute systemic illness, and he can be managed in the community (the urine dipstick, not the observations, answers the question of a UTI). Normal observations do not exclude pain in a child who cannot report it: the abdomen and the tooth are the clues.

handover.label: Bedside tests
handover.result: Urine dipstick, clean catch, and capillary blood glucose, taken in the clinic today.
handover.model: The urine is concentrated (specific gravity 1.025, at the top of the normal range), which fits his low fluid intake. Leucocytes, nitrites and blood are negative, so a UTI is unlikely and no antibiotics are needed; the extra wetting fits a loaded rectum pressing on the bladder. No glycosuria or ketonuria and a normal BGL of 5.2 mmol/L make diabetes very unlikely and exclude hypoglycaemia. It adds to the plan: more fluids as part of treating the constipation, and a urine culture only if urinary symptoms persist once he is disimpacted.

handover.label: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (teacher version)
handover.result:
Completed by his class teacher last week (teacher version, ages 4 to 17).

ScaleScoreBand (teacher cut-offs)
Emotional symptoms4 / 10Normal (0 to 4)
Conduct problems7 / 10Abnormal (4 to 10)
Hyperactivity and inattention9 / 10Abnormal (7 to 10)
Peer problems4 / 10Borderline (4)
Total difficulties (the four scales above)24 / 40Abnormal (16 to 40)
Prosocial behaviour3 / 10Abnormal, low (0 to 4)

Higher scores mean more difficulties, except prosocial behaviour, where a low score is the concern.

Teacher's comment: "A big change over the last month. He was settled and happy with his previous aide."
handover.model:
• The SDQ is a brief behavioural screening questionnaire for children and adolescents, with parent and teacher versions, covering emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity and inattention, peer problems and prosocial behaviour.
  • The teacher total of 24 is in the abnormal range, driven by conduct (7) and hyperactivity (9), with low prosocial behaviour (3); emotional symptoms are normal and peer problems borderline. It shows how marked his difficulties are now, and the teacher's comment says they are new.
  • It cannot say why: it is a screening and monitoring tool, not a diagnosis, and it does not exclude a physical cause. It was not designed for children with intellectual disability (the Developmental Behaviour Checklist was), and the high hyperactivity score may partly be akathisia from the risperidone increase.
  • So it does not justify a behaviour plan or more antipsychotic now: treat the constipation, the dental pain and the medication effects first, then repeat the SDQ to monitor change.

ask: You are now calling the paediatric registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Liam Nguyen, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Liam now, here in general practice.
Before Liam goes home, what would you tell his parent and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
Identify: self as the GP; Liam Nguyen, 10, 31 kg, moderate intellectual disability, largely non-verbal.

Situation: 3 weeks of worsening aggression, hitting his own tummy, poor sleep and appetite; I think pain is the cause.

Background: risperidone increased 6 weeks ago to 0.5 mg twice a day; hard stools every 4 to 5 days with soiling; no dental check for over 2 years; his aide left 4 weeks ago.

Assessment:

  • Observations normal, afebrile: no systemic infection; HR 104 with grimacing on left iliac fossa pressure fits pain.
  • Urine SG 1.025 is concentrated from low fluids; no leucocytes or nitrites, so UTI unlikely; BGL 5.2 normal.
  • SDQ total 24 is abnormal (conduct, hyperactivity): a screening tool that shows severity, not cause; hyperactivity may partly be akathisia.
  • Faecal loading, carious tender lower left molar, extrapyramidal signs.

Recommendation: manage in the community; advice on reducing risperidone; review in 1 to 2 weeks.

Most likely: pain-driven behaviour change from constipation with faecal loading and dental pain (probable dental abscess): hits his tummy, stools every 4 to 5 days with soiling, firm tender left iliac fossa mass; pulls at the left of his face, refuses crunchy food, carious tender molar with gum swelling.

  • Risperidone adverse effects: for: dose increase 6 weeks ago, cogwheel rigidity, tremor, drooling, akathisia that looks like agitation; it also worsens constipation.
  • Distress at losing his aide: for: aide and bus driver changed 4 weeks ago, teacher's comment; against: does not explain the pain signs.
  • UTI or reflux: UTI unlikely with a negative dipstick; reflux possible (arching, regurgitation).
  • Abuse or neglect: must be considered; against: no bruises, not fearful, parent denies harm.

1. Treat the physical causes first: no behaviour plan and no increase in antipsychotic.
  2. Constipation: oral macrogol disimpaction, increasing the daily sachets by age band as in the RCH constipation guideline table until stools are soft and runny, then maintenance for months; more fluids and fibre, a toileting routine.
  3. Dental: urgent paediatric or special needs dentistry referral (possibly treatment under anaesthetic); regular paracetamol 15 mg/kg = 465 mg up to 4 times a day and ibuprofen 10 mg/kg = 310 mg 8-hourly with food.
  4. Medication review: contact the prescriber to reduce risperidone towards the previous dose, not stop it abruptly; review the indication; no extra sedating medicine.
  5. Treat reflux if symptomatic.
  6. Involve: school (transition support, familiar staff, visual supports, behaviour plan on hold); carer support and respite; GP-led follow-up.
  7. Explain to the parent that pain is the likely cause, with empathy.

Tell the parent, in plain words: Liam's behaviour is most likely from pain in his tummy and tooth, and should settle once these are treated. Give the laxative and pain relief regularly.

Go to the Emergency Department or come back the same day if:

  • his face or neck swells, or he has a fever
  • he vomits, or his tummy is swollen or very painful
  • he has no bowel motion despite the laxatives
  • he develops new severe stiffness or abnormal movements after the risperidone change
  • call 000 if anyone is at immediate risk of harm

Follow-up: GP review in 1 to 2 weeks, sooner if worse, to check bowels, pain, behaviour and medication; confirm the dental appointment; repeat the SDQ once the physical causes are treated; arrange carer support and respite.

ddx.dx: Pain-driven behaviour change from constipation with faecal loading and dental pain (probable dental abscess)
ddx.for: He hits his tummy, passes hard stools every 4 to 5 days with soiling, has a firm tender left iliac fossa mass, pulls at the left of his face, refuses crunchy food and has a carious tender lower left molar with gum swelling.
ddx.against: He is afebrile with normal observations.

ddx.dx: Risperidone adverse effects (extrapyramidal effects, akathisia and constipation)
ddx.for: His risperidone was increased 6 weeks ago and since then he has cogwheel rigidity, tremor, drooling and restlessness that looks like agitation.
ddx.against: It does not explain his facial pulling or the tender molar with gum swelling.

ddx.dx: Distress at losing his familiar teacher's aide and bus driver
ddx.for: His long-standing aide and his bus driver both changed 4 weeks ago, and the teacher dates the change to the last month.
ddx.against: It does not explain his abdominal and dental pain signs.

ddx.for: He has been wetting a little more than usual.
ddx.against: He is afebrile and the dipstick is negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood.

ddx.for: He has had reflux since infancy and still arches his back and brings up food after meals.
ddx.against: It is long-standing and does not explain the new faecal loading or the tooth findings.

ddx.for: His parent is exhausted and at their limit, and he has a new relief aide and a new bus driver.
ddx.against: He has no bruises, is not fearful of anyone, and his parent denies harm and has no concerns about other carers.
